agent_5.question: Who holds the slot list and verifies each fisher’s logged catch weight?
agent_5.answer: I keep the slot list myself along with the other fishers – we agree on a rotating keeper who sets the 2‑hour slots for each round. After every trip, the keeper checks each fisher’s logged catch against the slot list and the lake’s updated stock. If someone reports more than 20 kg or the lake’s reserve falls below 12 % of the current stock, the keeper flags the violation and the community applies the fine and potential suspension.

It is recorded by the slot keeper and immediately added to the lake’s reserve pool – the shared stock that protects the community’s future. In practice, the keeper will take the excess catch, calculate 0.05 kg per kilogram over the limit, subtract that weight from my logged catch, and deposit the resulting fine weight into the reserve. I lose that amount from my own reserves, and the lake’s reserve grows by that amount.

agent_5.question: What exactly does the reserve pool refer to, and how is it tracked and maintained in relation to the lake’s total stock?
agent_5.answer:
The "reserve pool" is simply the portion of the lake’s stock that we agree to keep untouched for future use. It’s not a separate pond or container; it’s a bookkeeping construct that sits within the total lake stock. After every round, we subtract all logged catches from the lake’s current total, then we calculate 12 % of that remaining stock. That 12 % is the minimum reserve we must keep. We record the reserve as a counter on the ledger (the reserve pool). When a fisher exceeds his catch, the slot keeper levies a 0.05 kg fine per excess kilogram. That fine is first subtracted from the fisher’s personal reserve (so they can’t dip into the lake for that kg), and the fine’s weight is added back into the reserve pool. This keeps the reserve pool from shrinking and gives the community a quick way to see if the minimum threshold is being respected. The reserve pool is therefore tracked each round on the same ledger as the lake’s total stock, and the lake’s total stock is simply the sum of the reserve pool plus the usable fish.

This explanation doesn’t change any part of the proposal – it only clarifies how the reserve is handled.

agent_6.question: Who holds the communal reserve, and how is it tracked?
agent_6.answer: The reserve will be kept in a communal chest locked at the village council hall. Every fisher will drop his 5% deposit into the chest and write the amount on the ledger that sits on the wall of the hall. The ledger is signed by the fisher and the keeper, and copied weekly into the community notebook that everyone can see. That way we all know how much the reserve holds. If a fisher cannot pay a fine, the chest stays in the hall and the ledger records a 50% penalty for the next two trips.

If they exceed it, we write the fine (20% of the over‑catch) in the ledger and immediately subtract 20% from the allowance entry for that fisher so their next trip’s limit is reduced.

agent_2.question: Who is the rotating deposit keeper and how is the rotation determined?
agent_2.answer: The rotating deposit keeper is simply the fisher whose turn it is to act as the day’s custodian of the deposit ledger.  We decided that the rotation should be fair and transparent, so we agreed to use a simple alphabetical list of our last names (or a pre‑agreed list).  Each day, after the fishing ends, the next fisher on that list becomes keeper for the following day.  If a fisher is absent that day, we skip to the next one in line.  This keeps the responsibility shared and prevents any single person from bearing the burden for too long.
agent_2.revised_policy: No fisher may take more than 1.0 kg per trip, and the community may harvest no more than 10 % of the lake’s current stock per day.  A 0.1 kg refundable deposit is collected per trip and returned only if limits are respected.

After all trips, if every fisher’s catch ≤1.0 kg and total daily catch ≤10 % of lake stock, all deposits are refunded.  If any limit is breached, the deposit is forfeited and the fisher must either return the excess catch or pay a fine of 0.05 kg per kg over the limit.  The deposit keeper for the day is chosen by rotating among the fishers in alphabetical order; the keeper collects deposits, records catches, and audits the ledger.  If the keeper is absent, the next fisher in the rotation steps in.

agent_2.question: What happens to the deposit that is forfeited, and how are fines collected and distributed?
agent_2.answer:
If the limits are broken the deposit is not returned – it is moved into the community’s shared reserve.  That reserve is the same fund we use to pay for any maintenance on nets, boats and the shoreline, and to support small restoration projects for the lake.  When a fisher goes over the 1.0 kg per trip or the 10 % daily quota, the 0.1 kg deposit is taken out of his pocket and added to that reserve.  The fine of 0.05 kg per kg over the limit is collected in the same way – the keeper takes the amount from the fisher’s pocket and adds it to the reserve.  The keeper keeps a negligible administrative fee (0.01 kg) to cover the cost of keeping the ledger.  At the end of each month the reserve is reviewed; a portion is allocated for gear replacement and lake health work, and any remaining balance is split evenly among all fishers as a small community dividend.  This way the penalty money goes back to the community’s well‑being rather than vanishing.

agent_2.question: When is the daily 10% lake‑stock limit evaluated and how are total daily catches summed and compared to that limit?
agent_2.answer: The limit is checked at the close of the day, after the keeper has collected every deposit and logged every catch.  Each fisher reports his haul as soon as he returns, and the keeper adds those amounts as they come in.  When the last fisher of the day has finished, the keeper sums the totals for that day.  The comparison is made against 10 % of the lake’s stock as it existed at the start of that day (i.e., the stock before any of the day’s catches were removed).  If the summed haul is greater than that 10 % figure, the day is in breach and the deposit is forfeited and the excess is either returned or paid for with a 0.05 kg/kg fine.

agent_2.question: Who distributes the surplus from the reserve to fishers at the end of each month, and how is that distribution executed?

agent_3.question: What is the lake reserve, and how is the 35% deposit recorded and tracked—does it alter the community’s stock_kg state?
agent_3.answer:
The lake reserve is simply the portion of the lake’s stock that we agree to keep as a ‘bank’ for future use.  Whenever a fisher lands a catch, 35 % of that weight is immediately placed back into the lake.  That deposited mass is counted as part of the lake reserve and is included in the total stock_kg that the council monitors.  It does not add extra fish to the community’s reserve; it merely returns part of the catch to the lake so that the lake can recover.  The ledger records the catch weight before the trip, the 35 % deposit after landing, and the council checks the lake mass daily.  If the lake mass (including the reserve) drops below 9 kg, all fishing stops until it climbs to 14 kg.  Non‑compliance results in a 0.1 kg penalty on the next trip and possible temporary exclusion.

Thus the deposit does not alter the community’s stock_kg state beyond the normal removal of catch—it simply returns a portion back to the lake.  The reserve is a bookkeeping concept to remind us that part of the catch belongs in the lake for the long‑term benefit of all.

agent_3.question: What is the council and how does it enforce the suspension of fishing and the penalties for non‑compliance?
agent_3.answer:
The council is the community’s agreed‑upon body of fishermen and local elders who meet weekly to review the ledger and the lake’s mass.  The ledger is the single source of truth: every fisher writes down the weight of each catch before the trip, immediately deposits 35 % of that weight into the lake reserve, and the ledger is updated to show the new reserve balance and the fish taken.  On a daily basis the council or an elected steward tallies the total lake mass from the reserve plus any standing stock.  If that number falls below 9 kg, the council issues a communal notice that all fishing is suspended until the reserve reaches 14 kg.  The notice is posted on the shared board and a messenger reminds each fisher that they must stay aboard and refrain from landing any more fish until the mass threshold is met.  Failure to obey a suspension results in a 0.1 kg forfeiture from the next trip’s catch; repeated non‑compliance triggers temporary exclusion from fishing for one season.  The ledger records every violation and the forfeitures so that the council can enforce the penalties transparently and fairly.

agent_4.question: The proposal doesn't specify who enforces the ban on fishing for a week and how compliance is verified—who holds that enforcement authority and what mechanism ensures that a barred fisher does not fish during the suspension period?
agent_4.answer:
As Beti, I say that the enforcement of the ban falls to our own community council, with the volunteer biologist acting as the official verifier. After each trip, every fisher signs a catch slip and shows the exact amount of fish they brought in and the deposit they made. The biologist checks that the deposit matches the 0.08 kg per kg rule and records it in a communal ledger that sits on the dock. If a fisher fails to deposit or exceeds the 0.7 kg trip limit, the council reads the slip aloud, issues the fine, and writes the fisher’s name on a "no‑fishing" list that is posted on the community notice board. The fisher is then prohibited from leaving the dock for the next week, and the council, together with the biologist and two volunteer patrol members, will perform random checks at the dock to ensure the fisher is not attempting to fish. The same procedure applies to the whole community: if the total weekly catch exceeds 12 % of the lake’s stock, the council tallies the excess, imposes the community fine, and bans all fishers for a week, again enforced by the council and verified by the biologist and patrols. This way, the ban is enforced by people we trust and by a clear, publicly recorded system that everyone can see.

Our policy is based on sustainability, so we keep the catch limits tight, the deposit high enough to replenish the lake, and we make sure the enforcement is transparent and community‑driven.

By having the council, biologist, and patrol members work together, we create a simple, enforceable system that discourages cheating and protects the lake for future trips.

agent_5.question: How is the system supposed to detect when a fisher exceeds the 20 kg limit or violates the reserve, and who is responsible for automatically reducing that fisher’s quota by 20% for the next round?
agent_5.answer: We keep a shared logbook that every fisher updates after each trip. The log lists the lake’s stock at the start, the amount taken, and the remaining stock. The flagging is done by the community steward who, after verifying the entries, calls the fisher and the rest of the group. The steward records the violation and automatically applies a 20 % cut to that fisher’s quota for the next round in the ledger. If no one flags it, we trust the report, but if the steward finds a discrepancy, he’s responsible for the penalty.

agent_6.question: What is the process for restoring the deposit after an over‑quota catch, and who administers that process?
agent_6.answer: When a fisher exceeds the 40% quota, the next day the steward looks at the ledger and cuts that fisher’s trip allowance by 15%. The fisher then has to pay the full 5% deposit that would have gone into the communal reserve for that over‑quota trip. The deposit is paid to the steward on the following fishing day. Once the steward receives the deposit, the allowance is lifted back to normal for the next trip. If the deposit is not paid the allowance stays reduced until it is paid. The steward, elected by the council, is the one who administers the deposit collection and enforcement.

The deposit is paid on the following trip and collected by the community steward. The steward also monitors compliance and restores allowances when the deposit has been paid.

agent_7.question: What is the mechanism for collecting and deducting the 0.02 kg fine per missing kilogram from a fisher’s next catch or reserves, given that the proposal does not specify who holds reserves or how that deduction occurs?
agent_7.answer:
I’ll keep it simple: the monitor keeps a small ledger next to the lake’s logbook. Every time a fisher falls short of the 1 kg minimum, the monitor writes down the fine – 0.02 kg per missing kilo. When the fisher returns for the next trip, the monitor looks at that ledger and takes the fine out of the catch the fisher is about to submit. If the catch is smaller than the fine, the monitor will pull the remaining amount from the fisher’s personal reserve that we all keep in the communal storage bucket – the one we all drop off our spare catches in. If the reserve is also too low, the fisher has to pay the balance in trade or simply sit out until the fine clears. That way the fine is enforced without needing a separate bank.

The rule itself stays the same, but the operational detail about who holds reserves and how deductions happen is now spelled out.
agent_7.revised_policy: Each fisher may take up to 5 kg per trip, but the community must keep at least 25 % of the lake’s current stock untouched, and the total daily catch may not exceed 70 % of the lake’s weight; each fisher must bring at least 1 kg per trip or face a 0.02 kg fine.
agent_7.revised_operationalization: The community monitor records the lake weight at the start of each day. After all trips, fishers submit their catch. If a fisher is short, the monitor records a fine of 0.02 kg per missing kilogram in a shared ledger. On the fisher’s next trip, the monitor deducts the fine from the fisher’s catch. If the catch is insufficient to cover the fine, the remaining fine amount is deducted from the fisher’s personal reserve kept in the communal storage bucket. If the reserve also falls short, the fisher must settle the balance by trade or cannot fish until the fine is cleared.

I’m keeping the policy text the same but am adding that the reserve is held and updated on the ledger.

agent_9.question: The proposal says penalties are deducted from each fisher’s personal reserve, but it does not explain how that reserve is created, how fish are moved into or out of it, or how it is used to obtain fish from the lake. Who holds the reserve, how is it initialized, and how does it function in the day‑to‑day harvesting process?
agent_9.answer:
The reserve column on the ledger is simply a bookkeeping record of how many kilograms of fish a fisher has already removed from the lake and is holding in his own boat. It isn’t a separate pool of money or a credit line – it’s literally the weight of fish that the fisher owns. When I first join the community, my reserve starts at 0 kg. Whenever I go out and bring back fish, I add the actual catch to my reserve column. If I get a penalty, the keeper subtracts the penalty amount from my reserve and the excess fish are returned to the lake. The reserve is kept on the shared ledger by the keeper, who updates it after each trip and after any penalties are applied. In day‑to‑day fishing, I simply look at my reserve to see how much fish I already have on board; I can keep those fish until I sell them. I never ‘borrow’ fish from the reserve – I only take fish from the lake up to the rule’s limits and then record the catch. The reserve is only used to record the fish I’ve taken and to enforce penalties; it is not a separate account used to obtain fish from the lake.

This means the reserve is held in the ledger, created at 0 kg at the start of each season, increased by every catch I take, and decreased only by penalties. The keeper is the only one who updates it.

There is no separate ‘deposit’ account for fish; the 0.1 kg deposit that is paid each trip goes into a common deposit tank that is not part of the reserve column.

If the reserve is misunderstood or if we need to formalise that the reserve represents physically owned fish, we can adjust the wording accordingly.

So the reserve is just a record of the fish I keep in my boat; it is created when I first take fish, it is updated by adding each catch and subtracting penalties, and it is maintained on the shared ledger by the keeper.

I hope that clears up how the reserve works.

agent_3.question: Who holds the lake reserve deposits and manages the reserve?
agent_3.answer: The deposits go into the lake reserve, a communal pool that’s held in trust by the Community Fishing Council.  Each fisher records their catch on the shared ledger and the 30 % deposit is immediately put into that pool.  The Council, elected by all of us, manages the reserve—keeping a physical or digital record, overseeing any use of the funds (restocking, maintenance, or redistributing to those who need it), and ensuring the reserve never runs out.  In short, it’s a community‑owned deposit, managed by the Council that all fishers trust and that we all can audit on the ledger.

At the end of each season, the total catch is tallied; if any fisher exceeds 4 kg total, they pay a fine and must return the excess to the reserve.  Non‑compliance triggers a 0.05 kg fine per kilogram of over‑take, and repeat offenders are temporarily banned for one season.

agent_6.question: The proposal states that fishers must deposit 5% of their catch into a communal reserve, but it does not specify who holds that reserve, how it is tracked, or how it is used to determine when the reserve falls below 5 kg or rises to 10 kg.
agent_6.answer: I reckon the reserve should sit in a communal chest or jar right in the community hall. Each fisher brings in their 5 % deposit there and signs the ledger that shows how much the reserve is at. The senior fishers—our council—check that ledger each morning, tally the weight, and let everyone know if the reserve is under 5 kg or has reached 10 kg so we can adjust the next trip’s take. That way everyone knows exactly who holds the reserve, how it’s tracked, and when the thresholds kick in.
agent_6.revised_policy: Each fisher may take up to 35 % of the lake’s current biomass per trip and must deposit 5 % of their catch into a communal reserve. The reserve will be held in a secure chest at the community hall and its balance recorded in a shared ledger signed by each fisher at the time of deposit. If the reserve falls below 5 kg, the allowable take for every fisher will be reduced by 5 % of the lake’s current biomass on the following trip. This reduction will continue, trip‑by‑trip, until the reserve rises to at least 10 kg, at which point the standard 35 % allowance is restored. Violations of the deposit rule are fined 0.02 kg per kilogram short and the catch is returned to the lake.

They will all have equal voting power, and each will sign the ledger and weigh the reserve once per day. This keeps the process simple and ensures nobody has permanent control.

agent_7.question: Who is responsible for collecting and holding the communal fine pool?
agent_7.answer: The rotating monitor will be the one to collect the excess‑catch fines and hold the fine pool until the weekly distribution, so that the community can enforce the 30% reserve and 60% total catch limits.  The monitor will also keep an eye on the ledger to make sure the pool is used correctly.  In short, it’s the monitor’s responsibility to gather and hold the fine pool.

Every trip a fisher records the catch on a shared ledger and deposits any weight beyond 4 kg into a communal fine pool.  The community sums the daily ledger to enforce the 60 % limit; if the total exceeds it or the reserve dips below 30 %, the fine pool is distributed to replenish the lake or to those who caught less than 1 kg.  Fines of 0.05 kg per kg over the limits are imposed for non‑compliance.  All records are checked by a rotating monitor each week.

The ledger is posted daily for transparency and is audited weekly by the monitor.  No changes to the rest of the operationalization.

agent_7.question: How is the fine pool allocated between lake replenishment and compensation to low‑catch fishers, and who decides that distribution?
agent_7.answer: The fine pool is first used to restore the lake to the required 30 % reserve level. Once that target is met, any leftover money is paid out to fishers who caught less than 1 kg, in proportion to how much they fell short of the 1 kg minimum. The rotating monitor collects all fines, calculates the reserve‑replenishment amount and the low‑catch payout, and presents the split to the community each week. The community then approves the distribution. This ensures the lake’s reserve is protected while also compensating those who are unable to meet the minimum catch.

agent_7.question: How does the community check and enforce the 60 % total catch limit, and what happens if the limit is exceeded?
agent_7.answer: Every round we log each fisher’s catch to the shared ledger. At the end of the round we sum all catches and compare that total to 60 % of the lake’s weight at the start of the round. If the sum exceeds 60 %, the excess amount is treated as a fine: 0.05 kg of fine is collected per kg over the 60 % limit and added to the communal fine pool. The pool is first used to replenish the lake so it meets the 30 % reserve requirement. If the pool is not enough, the remaining fines are split among fishers who caught less than 1 kg, proportional to their shortfall. When the limit is exceeded we also pause further fishing for that round until the lake has reached the 30 % reserve, and we adjust the next day’s quota downward if necessary to protect the lake.

agent_3.answer: We’ll keep track of the lake’s weight by recording every catch and deposit in the communal ledger. When the next weekly check shows the lake mass has reached 12 kg or more, the steward will lift the suspension and the fishers can resume. If the pot has enough to give that fisher back 0.05 kg on the same day, we do it. If not, the fine is carried over and simply deducted from the fisher’s next catch. agent_7.question: How is the communal pool tracked in state and how are reimbursements applied to a fisher’s payoff when funds are available?
agent_7.answer: The communal pool is kept as a single numeric balance in the community ledger ("pool_balance"). Whenever a 0.05 kg fine is levied, I add that amount to pool_balance. When a fisher’s catch is logged and a fine is due, I first check pool_balance. If pool_balance is greater than or equal to the fine amount, I deduct that amount from pool_balance and credit the same amount to the fisher’s personal payoff account, effectively reimbursing them. If the pool is insufficient, the fine is carried forward and added to pool_balance later. The balance is visible to all fishers and persists day‑to‑day until the next communal meeting. Thus reimbursements are applied directly against the pool balance, ensuring that the total funds collected from fines can be used to return money to those who under‑report their catch.
